title: Building the cocktail menu
lead: Shape the list, price it, change it with the seasons, and read what sells.

sections.name: Menu engineering

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Sort every drink by how often it sells and what it earns.

know: Star sells a lot, earns a lot: keep it.
Plowhorse sells a lot, earns little: fix the cost or price.
Puzzle earns a lot, sells little: move or promote it.
Dog neither: rework or remove it.

keyPoints.line: the ones guests ask for, each covered.
bright, stirred, tall, and one without spirit.
every drink, so a server can sell it.

read.bigIdea: A menu covers the guests, not the bartender.
read.where: Start from who orders. Cover the **base spirits** guests ask for, then a range of **styles**: bright and shaken, strong and stirred, tall and bubbly, and at least one **spiritless** drink. Mix **easy sellers** with one or two drinks worth talking about. Every drink gets a **name** a guest can say and **one line** a server can sell it with.

stops.name: Spirits
stops.text: Is every spirit guests ask for **covered**?

stops.name: Words
stops.text: A name and **one line** for each.

read.mixup: Eight sours with different names is one drink, eight times. Cover the **styles**, not just the spirits.
read.sayIt: There’s something for every taste: tell me what you usually like.

keyPoints.line: no drink far off its neighbors without a reason.

read.bigIdea: Price from cost, then fit the menu.
read.where: Each drink is priced from its **cost**: price = cost ÷ the **target pour cost**. Bar guides put a common target at about **18–25%** for spirits and cocktails, and it varies by bar. Then look at the list as a whole: prices should step up for a reason a guest can see (a rarer bottle, a bigger pour), not because one drink happened to cost more.
read.mixup: A low pour cost isn’t always the best drink to sell. A $16 drink at 25% can earn more dollars than a $10 drink at 18%.
read.sayIt: This one’s a little more because it’s made with a rare rye.

keyPoints.line: the drinks that sell all year.
a few for what’s in season.
before the new menu goes live.

read.bigIdea: Change part of the list, keep what sells.
read.where: A seasonal change swaps **some** drinks for ones built on what’s in season (stone fruit in summer, apple and spice in fall), and **keeps** the drinks guests come back for. Every new drink gets a **written spec**, a **cost**, and a **price** before it goes on. The team is **trained** on it before the first guest can order it.

stops.name: Train
stops.text: Every bartender and server **tastes the idea** and learns the line.

read.mixup: A new menu isn’t done when the drinks are. It’s done when the **team** can sell them.
read.sayIt: It’s new for the season: a fall drink with apple and spice.

keyPoints.line: sells a lot, earns a lot: keep it.
sells a lot, earns little: fix the cost or price.
earns a lot, sells little: move or promote it.

read.bigIdea: Sort every drink by how often it sells and what it earns.
read.where: Menu engineering comes from **Michael Kasavana and Donald Smith** (Michigan State University, 1982). Each item is scored two ways: **popularity** (how many sell) and **contribution margin** (price minus cost, in dollars). That puts it in one of four boxes: **Stars**, **Plowhorses**, **Puzzles** and **Dogs**.

stops.name: Plowhorse
stops.text: Popular, low margin: **reprice** or cut cost.

stops.name: Puzzle
stops.text: High margin, rarely ordered: **reposition** or promote.

read.mixup: Margin here is **dollars**, not pour-cost percent. A drink can have a great percentage and still earn few dollars.

sources: Kasavana and Smith, Menu Engineering (1982), as summarized by AHLEI, “The Power of Menu Engineering” (ahlei.servsafebrands.com); Level 3, Costing and the menu: BevSpot and Backbar Academy pour-cost guides; House practice (ours; GM to confirm). Written for Mise in our own words, Nov 12, 2026.
